content: The kilogram, symbolized as kg, is the fundamental unit of mass in the International System of Units (SI). It is uniquely defined as the mass of the International Prototype Kilogram (IPK), a physical artifact made of a platinum-iridium alloy. The kilogram is the only SI base unit that incorporates a prefix in its name and remains defined by a physical object rather than a fundamental physical constant. The IPK's mass is nearly equivalent to the mass of one liter of water. However, the kilogram's reliance on a physical artifact has led to challenges in maintaining its stability over time. For instance, the IPK has been observed to vary slightly in mass when compared to its official copies distributed worldwide. For example, an object with a mass of one kilogram will accelerate at one meter per second squared when subjected to a force of one newton. Unlike weight, which depends on local gravitational strength, mass remains constant regardless of location. Historically, the kilogram was initially defined in 1795 as the mass of one cubic decimeter of water at its maximum density (approximately 4°C). However, practical limitations led to the creation of a metallic prototype, which became the standard for the kilogram. In 1889, the IPK was formally adopted as the international standard, replacing earlier definitions. Any change in the kilogram's definition would cascade through these units, affecting their values. Efforts to redefine the kilogram have explored various approaches, including fixing the value of the Planck constant or the Avogadro constant. These methods aim to base the kilogram on invariant natural constants, enabling its realization in laboratories worldwide without reliance on a single physical artifact. Despite these advancements, achieving the required precision for a new definition remains a challenge. Current methods, such as the watt balance and silicon sphere experiments, are approaching the necessary level of accuracy but have not yet surpassed the stability of the IPK. As a result, the kilogram continues to be defined by the IPK, though its eventual redefinition is anticipated to align with the broader trend of basing SI units on fundamental constants.
